title: Government Vocabulary: Systems and Concepts
summary: Words for how a country is governed: democracy, democratic, national policy, revenue, bureaucracy and agency.

p: A register is the special vocabulary used in a particular area of life, such as government and administration. These are the exact terms used in political talk, news reports, legal documents and civic life. Knowing them helps you with comprehension passages and with discussing political and social issues clearly. We group the words by theme.

Democracy: a system of government in which power belongs to the people, who use it directly or through elected representatives. Example: Nigeria's return to democracy in 1999 ended decades of military rule. Think of a general election in which citizens queue to vote.

Democratic: an adjective that describes anything connected with or supporting the principles of democracy: fairness, equality and popular participation. Example: The selection of the student council was highly democratic, with a secret ballot and open debates.

National policy: a plan or course of action begun, accepted and followed by a country's government. Example: The new national policy on agriculture aims at food security by encouraging local rice production.

Revenue: the total income of a government, from taxes, customs duties and the sale of natural resources. Example: A large part of the government's revenue comes from crude oil exports. Compare expenditure: the money a government spends.

Bureaucracy: the complex structure of government officials, departments and procedures. It is often criticised as slow and bound by too many rules, which is called red tape. Example: Getting a passport can be frustrating because of the layers of bureaucracy.

Agency: a specific government department or organisation responsible for one area of public service. Example: The National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) protects Nigeria's environment.
Democracy is a noun. Democratic is an adjective. Democratically is an adverb. Democratise is a verb. Bureaucracy (noun) gives bureaucratic (adjective) and bureaucrat (a person).

title: Government Vocabulary: Official Documents and Meetings
summary: White paper, gazette, circular, memorandum, agenda and minutes, and the difference between an agenda and minutes.

p: White paper: an official government report that states policy or gives the final response to the findings of a committee or commission of inquiry. It shows the government's official position and what it will do. Example: After the panel investigated the disaster, the state government issued a White Paper accepting all its recommendations.

Gazette: an official government publication used to announce public notices, new laws, appointments and orders. To publish something in it is to gazette it. Example: The new judges will start work only after their names have been gazetted.

Circular: a formal letter or notice sent to many people or departments at the same time so that all take the same action or receive the same information. Example: A circular from the Ministry of Education told all principals about the new school calendar.

Memorandum (memo): a short, informal written message for communication inside an organisation, to inform, remind or request. Example: The Head of Department sent a memo reminding all staff of the project deadline.

Agenda: a list of the items to be discussed at a formal meeting. It gives structure and makes sure that all topics are covered. Example: The first item on the agenda of the parents' meeting was the proposed increase in school fees.

Minutes: the official written record of what happened at a meeting: the discussions, decisions and actions agreed. They are usually approved at the next meeting. Example: The secretary was asked to take the minutes.
The difference: the agenda is written BEFORE the meeting and says what will be discussed. The minutes are written DURING or AFTER the meeting and say what was discussed and decided.

sections.h: Typical order of a formal meeting
p: Call to order and opening prayer; reading and approval of the minutes of the last meeting; matters arising; the main items; any other business; the date of the next meeting; closing.

activity: Explain the difference between an agenda and minutes. What is the purpose of a white paper? What is the verb that means 'to publish in the official journal' (to gazette)?

title: Government Vocabulary: Personnel, Structure and Practice
summary: Permanent secretary, cadre and official rank, followed by practice exercises with all the words from Weeks 1 and 2.

p: Permanent Secretary: the most senior non-political civil servant, the administrative head of a government ministry. The Minister, who is a politician, decides the policy direction, and the Permanent Secretary is responsible for carrying it out and for the day-to-day running of the ministry. Example: The new Minister of Health met the Permanent Secretary to learn about the ministry's problems.

Cadre: a small group of people trained for a particular purpose or with a particular skill, especially in an organisation with ranks such as the civil service or the army. Example: After her promotion she joined the senior management cadre of the federal civil service.

Official rank: a person's formal position or grade in a structured hierarchy such as the army, police or civil service. It shows the level of authority and responsibility. Example: Despite his high official rank, he was known for his humble manner.

Fill in the gaps using: policy, agency, agenda, minutes, circular. The Permanent Secretary sent a (a) circular to all staff, informing them of a new government (b) policy on transportation. To discuss its implementation, a meeting was called. The first item on the (c) agenda was to read the (d) minutes of the last meeting. It was announced that the policy would be carried out by a new (e) agency created for that purpose.

Governing systems: democracy, democratic, national policy, revenue, bureaucracy, agency. Documents: white paper, gazette, circular, memorandum, agenda, minutes. Personnel: Permanent Secretary, cadre, official rank. Practise using each in a sentence about an event in the news.

title: Spoken English: Reading and Appreciating Poetry
summary: How to read a poem aloud: rhythm and metre, rhyme, tone and intonation, punctuation and enjambment.

p: Reading poetry aloud is interpretation, not just recitation. You must pay attention to its prosody, the patterns of rhythm and sound.

Rhythm is the heartbeat of a poem: the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Finding the metre, such as iambic pentameter, helps you find the natural beat. An iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one; pentameter means five of them in a line.
Example: Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY? The line has ten syllables: weak, strong, weak, strong, and so on. Tip: read aloud and tap on the desk at each stressed syllable.
Rhyme is the repetition of similar sounds, usually at the ends of lines. The rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhymes, marked with letters. A Shakespearean sonnet usually follows ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.
Your voice must show the mood or tone of the poem: sad, sarcastic, joyful or thoughtful. Use a rising tone for uncertainty or questions and a falling tone for statements and a sense of finality.

Do not stop at the end of every line. Pause only where there is punctuation (commas, full stops, semicolons). Enjambment is when a sentence runs from one line into the next without a pause. Example: Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments. The thought continues across the line break. Reading with enjambment is like driving over small hills: you keep your speed and do not stop at the top of each one.

activity: Choose a poem from your literature text. Mark the stressed syllables in one stanza, find its rhyme scheme and note where there is enjambment. Then read it aloud, pausing only at punctuation.

title: Arguing Effectively and Following Arguments
summary: How to build a strong argument (contention, logos, ethos, pathos, rebuttal) and how to follow and judge someone else's argument, including logical fallacies.

p: A formal argument is a structured way of persuading. It is not a quarrel. It needs both the skill to build a case and the skill to take another case apart.

sections.h: Building an argument as a speaker
p: 1. A clear contention (thesis): one debatable statement. Example: This house believes that single-use plastics should be banned immediately.
2. Logical reasoning (logos): evidence, data and logical steps. Example: Only 9% of all the plastic ever produced has been recycled, so a ban is a logical necessity.
3. Ethical appeal (ethos): show that you are credible and that your position is moral. Example: As future custodians of this planet, we have an ethical duty to act.

4. Emotional appeal (pathos): connect with the audience's feelings, but use it sparingly to support logic, not replace it. Example: Imagine sea creatures choking on this plastic. This is the legacy we are creating.
5. Rebuttal: expect and answer the other side's main points. Example: They will say a ban is inconvenient, but is convenience worth the permanent destruction of our environment?

sections.h: Following an argument as a listener
p: Identify the core: what is the speaker's central claim? Map the structure: what are the main supporting points, the pillars? Evaluate the evidence: are the examples relevant and the statistics believable? Spot logical fallacies, which are errors of reasoning, such as a personal attack on the speaker instead of the idea (ad hominem) or an exaggerated chain of consequences (slippery slope).

Useful phrases: I strongly believe that..., The evidence clearly shows..., My opponent has argued that... but this overlooks..., In conclusion, we maintain... Speak slowly, face the audience and support every claim.

activity: Prepare a one-minute speech for or against: School uniforms should be abolished. Include a contention, one reason with evidence, one emotional appeal and one rebuttal. Identify which of your sentences are logos, pathos and rebuttal.

title: Writing for Different Audiences
summary: How purpose, tone and register change when you write to a teacher or principal and when you write to a newspaper, with model openings.

p: The same information must be written differently for different readers. This is a matter of register (the level of language) and tone (the attitude).

sections.h: Writing to your teacher or principal
p: Purpose: to request, explain or apologise formally. Tone: respectful and polite. Register: standard formal English, no contractions (write cannot, not can't), with correct titles and salutations.
Model opening: Dear Mr. Adekunle, I am writing to respectfully request a brief meeting to discuss my academic progress in your subject...

sections.h: Writing to a newspaper or magazine
p: Purpose: to inform, persuade or complain in a public place. Tone: formal, objective and confident, because you are speaking to a wide, unknown readership. Register: clear, direct and forceful. Get to the point quickly and do not assume that readers know you or the situation.
Model opening (letter to the editor): Sir, I wish to draw public attention to the deplorable and increasingly dangerous state of the Oron Road, which has been neglected for over a year...

Salutation: Dear Sir or Dear Madam or Dear Mr. Name to a person you know; Sir or Dear Editor for a newspaper letter. Tone: deferential to a principal; confident and objective to the public. Content: with the principal you can refer to personal details; for a newspaper, give the facts of a matter of public interest.

sections.h: A short model letter (to the principal)
p: Dear Sir, I am writing respectfully to ask for a testimonial in support of my application for the State Scholarship. I have been a student of this school for six years and have been a member of the Debating Society and the Science Club. I would be grateful if the testimonial could be ready by the end of the month, because the application closes on the fifteenth of next month. I thank you for your time and consideration. Yours faithfully, (name), SS3A.

activity: Write a letter of about 100 words to your Principal requesting a testimonial for a scholarship. Then write the first three sentences of a letter to a newspaper complaining about refuse in your street. Compare the tone of the two.

title: Grammar: Adjuncts (Forms and Functions)
summary: What an adjunct is, and its five main functions: time, place, manner, reason and frequency.

p: An adjunct is a word, phrase or clause that gives extra (optional) information about the action in a sentence. It acts as an adverbial and gives context. A test: if you remove it, the sentence is still grammatically complete. (She wrote the letter quickly. Without quickly the sentence is still complete.) Be careful: some adverbials are required by the verb and cannot be removed, as in He put the book on the table. These are not true adjuncts.
An adjunct may be one word (tomorrow), a phrase (in the main hall) or a clause (because it rained).
1. Time: answers When? or How long? The meeting will begin tomorrow. She lived in Kano for five years.
2. Place: answers Where? They held the concert in the main hall. Please wait outside.
3. Manner: answers How? In what way? He completed the task with incredible efficiency. She spoke confidently.
4. Reason: answers Why? The match was postponed because of heavy rain. Because of the traffic, I was late.
5. Frequency: answers How often? I always review my notes after class. We have meetings twice a week.

In She worked diligently throughout the night: diligently is an adjunct of manner, and throughout the night is an adjunct of time (how long). Ask the questions when, where, how, why and how often of the verb to find the adjuncts.

activity: Write one sentence for each type of adjunct (time, place, manner, reason, frequency) and underline the adjunct. Identify the adjuncts in: They sometimes play football on the field after school.

title: Reading: Paraphrasing Drama
summary: How to paraphrase dramatic passages written in older English, with worked examples from Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet.

p: To paraphrase is to say a text again in your own words while keeping its meaning and feeling. In drama this is hard because of subtext (the unspoken meaning behind the words) and old-fashioned (archaic) language.

1. Read the passage carefully to understand its overall meaning and emotion. 2. Find the meaning of unfamiliar or old words: thou (you), thee (you), thy (your), hath (has), art (are), wherefore (why), 'tis (it is), wilt (will). 3. Rewrite the passage in modern standard English, keeping the character's intention, not just the literal words.

Original: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles, and by opposing end them?

Paraphrase: The basic choice is between going on living and choosing death. Is it more honourable to patiently endure the endless pain and unfairness that life throws at you, or to fight back against all your troubles, even if the fight ends in your death?
Original: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse thy name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, and I'll no longer be a Capulet.
Notice that wherefore means why, not where. Juliet is not asking where Romeo is. She is asking why he has to be a Montague, the family that is the enemy of hers.
Paraphrase: Romeo, why do you have to be Romeo, a Montague? Give up your father and your name, or if you will not, simply promise to love me and I will stop being a Capulet.

activity: Paraphrase the following from Romeo and Juliet into one clear modern sentence: What's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. (A name is only a label; a thing is what it is whatever it is called.)
